title: The Character of Jesus
short: the argument from the character of Jesus

keyTerms.d: Lord, liar, or lunatic: such claims cannot be made innocently, so either the claims are true, or the man who made them was profoundly dishonest, or he was profoundly deranged. Made famous by C. S. Lewis, who popularized it rather than inventing it.

The objection Lewis never named: if the high self-claims are the developed theology of a later community placed on his lips, the dilemma dissolves. Run honestly, the argument is a tetralemma, and legend must be closed with evidence before the other three are weighed.

Forgiving sins that were not committed against him (Mark 2:5–7), placing his own words above the Torah (Matthew 5:21–22), making every person’s eternal destiny turn on their response to him (Matthew 10:32–33), and returning as the world’s judge (Mark 8:38).
Keeping Jesus as a tame ethical sage while quietly discarding the claims that gave his ethics their authority. The character and the claims come as a package, and the package will not be unwrapped.

The earliest Christians make a claim about Jesus that they make about no one else and that ancient literature almost never makes about anyone: that he was sinless — a verdict rendered not by distant admirers but by Jews steeped in a tradition that insisted all have sinned.

The same Gospels that call Jesus sinless preserve scenes a community merely burnishing its founder had less reason to keep. They do not prove sinlessness; the narrower point is that the record was not sanitized, which is what makes its verdict worth weighing at all.

The argument need not treat the Gospels as uniformly reliable or wholly unreliable: it takes what critical scholarship grants on ordinary grounds — multiple attestation, embarrassment, coherence with a first-century Jewish setting — and asks what best explains it.

Not a freestanding proof: the argument’s force is genuinely conditional on prior conclusions about Gospel reliability. If the portrait is substantially trustworthy, a powerful coherence emerges; it does not manufacture that trust from nothing.

derive.q: He forgives sins committed against others, sets his word above the Torah, and makes every person’s destiny turn on their response to him — so such claims…?
derive.why: A morally good and mentally sound human being does not go about implying that he is the hinge of history and the rightful object of worship. Either the claims are true, or the man who made them was profoundly dishonest, or he was profoundly deranged — and the second and third options sit very badly indeed with the moral portrait.

derive.q: The same Gospels that call him sinless keep his family saying “he is out of his mind,” his anguish in Gethsemane, and his cry of abandonment — so the record…?
derive.ans: was not sanitized (which is not yet proof of sinlessness)
derive.why: Their survival is at least consistent with a memory reported rather than manufactured, though a critic will fairly note they also serve Mark’s own theology of the suffering righteous one. Being thought mad, or afraid, or forsaken is not a sin; the narrower point is that the record was not sanitized, which is what makes its verdict worth weighing at all.

derive.q: A messianic fraud had a ready script — a conquering son of David — yet the message centred on a cross the Law called accursed — so the ‘liar’ horn…?
derive.ans: bears hard on deliberate deception (it does not prove the claims true)
derive.why: A calculated lie is shaped to be believed. A fraud angling to be received as Israel’s deliverer does not court the one outcome most certain to discredit him before the very people he is trying to win. The argument requires only that a crucified messiah stood at the centre of the movement’s message from the first — and a sceptic can hardly doubt that the cross was there, and unwelcome, from the start.

derive.q: A man of penetrating psychological insight, who warned relentlessly against pride, catastrophically self-deceived at the centre of his self-understanding — so the ‘lunatic’ horn is…?
derive.ans: improbable on the evidence — not refuted by definition
derive.why: It is stranger still that such a delusion left no other mark on a life his intimates judged blameless. The defender must concede that grandiosity and sanctity have, on rare occasions, coexisted. But the conjunction is improbable, and improbability is what evidential arguments trade in.

derive.q: The forgiving of sins, the reinterpretation of the Law, and the summons to judgment are in Mark, and Marana tha is Aramaic and pre-Pauline — so the legend exit…?
derive.ans: is not free: the high claims are not confined to John
derive.why: The trilemma’s premise does not stand or fall with the Fourth Gospel alone. The earliest layer we can reach answers the legend thesis directly: the pattern of worship is in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion, not a century after. John is not the invention of a new doctrine but the most explicit articulation of an old one.

derive.q: Grant all of it. Does the argument from character, by itself, prove the deity of Christ?
derive.ans: no — it forecloses the middle, and its verdict rests on wider grounds
derive.why: It does not, by itself, establish that the Gospels are reliable, that the resurrection occurred, or that the high self-claims are authentic rather than developed. Its first and surest work is narrower: it forecloses the comfortable middle position. It rests on the reliability of the Gospel portrait, and its decisive confirmation is the resurrection; both are argued elsewhere.

honestState.p1: It would be misleading to suggest the trilemma enjoys broad scholarly endorsement as a proof; it does not. Among professional New Testament scholars and philosophers of religion, Lewis’s formulation is often judged rhetorically powerful but logically incomplete precisely because of the legend objection, and the question of Jesus’s self-understanding remains genuinely contested. The debate is live, but it is not evenly balanced: the disagreement over the earliest Christology is not really about dates but about what kind of being the earliest Christians took him to be, and the earliest worship answers that question. The argument from character draws on the maximalist side of the ledger.
honestState.fairness: Lewis was right that Jesus will not stay in the box we build for him; where he was perhaps too quick was in suggesting he had left us only three doors. There is a fourth. And every link in the chain depends on source-judgments a reasonable person can weigh differently — the Sanhedrin scene in particular is among the most contested in the Gospels and is not offered as bedrock; what is bedrock is that Jesus was executed on a messianic charge, “The King of the Jews.” But the fourth door does not lead, as the skeptic hopes, back to the safe and tepid sage. It leads into the hardest and most interesting question in all of history: what kind of man was actually remembered, and why those who remembered him remembered a man in whom they found no flaw.
honestState.verdict: Not a proof of the deity of Christ, and not a knock-down refutation of the sceptic — but the earliest sources we can reach already remember a man who forgave sins as only God can, and his character fits neither a liar nor a madman. Our conclusion is that his claims were true: he is, as the Church has always confessed, fully God and fully man, two natures in one person — the Christ whose character compels is the same Christ who wept, hungered and died. The argument from character does not carry that weight alone; it rests on the reliability of the Gospel portrait, and its decisive confirmation is the resurrection. Within those bounds, its verdict is not “possibly Lord.” It is Lord.

order: Jesus claimed divine prerogatives — already in Mark, not confined to John — so he was a liar, a lunatic, or Lord.
Liar and lunatic sit very badly indeed with the moral portrait.
Therefore his claims were true: he is Lord, fully God and fully man.

cards.q: State Premise 1 — and its honest limit.
cards.a: Jesus claimed divine prerogatives — so he was either deceiving (liar), deluded (lunatic), or right (Lord); merely ‘a great moral teacher’ is not on the menu his claims allow. Limit: the most explicit claims are Johannine, so the argument’s force is conditional on Gospel reliability.

cards.q: State Premise 2 — and how strong a claim “very badly indeed” is.
cards.a: Liar and lunatic sit very badly indeed with the moral portrait. The argument’s claim is evidential, not deductive — improbability is what evidential arguments trade in.

cards.q: What does the conclusion reach — and what does it rest on?
cards.a: That his claims were true: he is Lord, fully God and fully man — not one at the expense of the other. It rests on the reliability of the Gospel portrait, with the resurrection as its decisive confirmation; the argument from character does not carry that weight alone.

cards.q: Why is ‘a great moral teacher, but not God’ not an option?
cards.a: Because such claims cannot be made innocently: a morally good and mentally sound human being does not go about implying that he is the hinge of history and the rightful object of worship. The character and the claims come as a package, and the package will not be unwrapped.

cards.q: What is the argument’s first and surest work?
cards.a: Narrower than a proof: it forecloses the comfortable middle position. You may decide he was a fraud; you may decide he was mad; you may fall at his feet. What you may not do is keep him as a tame ethical sage while quietly discarding the claims that gave his ethics their authority.

cards.q: Why does the sinlessness claim carry weight?
cards.a: The earliest Christians make it about Jesus and about no one else, and ancient literature almost never makes it about anyone. And it was rendered not by distant admirers but by Jews steeped in a tradition that insisted all have sinned.

cards.q: Why do the unflattering scenes matter — and what do they not prove?
cards.a: His family saying he was out of his mind, his anguish in Gethsemane, his cry of abandonment: a community merely burnishing its founder had less reason to keep them. They do not prove sinlessness — being thought mad, or afraid, or forsaken is not a sin — but they show the record was not sanitized.

cards.q: How does the cross bear on the ‘liar’ horn — and how little does the point require?
cards.a: A deliberate deceiver chooses a more sellable story; a fraud angling to be Israel’s deliverer does not court a death the Law called accursed. The point requires only that a crucified messiah stood at the centre of the message from the first — not that Jesus foresaw the manner of his death in detail.

cards.q: Why is the ‘lunatic’ horn improbable — and what must the defender concede?
cards.a: A man who diagnosed self-deception in others with surgical precision would have to be catastrophically self-deceived at the centre of his self-understanding, with no other mark on a life his intimates judged blameless. Concede: grandiosity and sanctity have, on rare occasions, coexisted.

The high claims are not confined to John: the forgiving of sins, the reinterpretation of the Law and the summons to judgment are in Mark, our earliest Gospel; and the earliest worship — Marana tha, Aramaic and pre-Pauline — is in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion. John is the most explicit articulation of an old doctrine, not a new one.

cards.q: In the trial material, what is contested and what is bedrock?
cards.a: The reported Sanhedrin exchange is among the most contested scenes in the Gospels and is not offered as bedrock. What is bedrock, independent of the dialogue, is that Jesus was executed on a messianic charge — the notice over the cross read “The King of the Jews” — a datum even sceptical historians grant.

cards.q: Reply to: the argument is circular — the same Gospels supply both the claims and the character.
cards.a: It need not treat the Gospels as uniformly reliable or wholly unreliable. On ordinary critical grounds the broad moral character and the implicit authority-claims are well-rooted in the tradition, while specific Johannine formulations get more caution; the argument takes what critical scholarship grants and asks what best explains it — layered, not viciously circular.

obj.q: The trilemma is a false dilemma: liar, lunatic, Lord — or legend. The exalted claims are in John, the latest Gospel, a later community’s theology placed on his lips.
obj.model: The concession is real and should not be hurried past: if the divine self-understanding of Jesus were entirely a Johannine overlay, the trilemma would not survive as a proof. But the high claims are not confined to John. The forgiving of sins, the sovereign reinterpretation of the Law, the summons to make him the criterion of judgment — these are in Mark, our earliest Gospel. Jesus was executed on a messianic charge, “The King of the Jews,” a datum even sceptical historians grant. And Marana tha is Aramaic, pre-Pauline, rooted in the earliest Aramaic-speaking churches, with the pattern of worship in place within a decade or two of the crucifixion. John is not the invention of a new doctrine but the most explicit articulation of an old one.

obj.q: The ‘lunatic’ horn is a caricature. History is full of admirable, sane, sincere people who were profoundly mistaken about themselves. He could simply have been tragically wrong.
obj.model: Here Christianity can afford to be generous: the sincerely mistaken sage is a hypothesis to be weighed on the evidence, not dismissed by definition — and it is precisely the hypothesis the moral portrait makes harder to sustain. A man may be sincerely deluded about a metaphysical fact. It is stranger for a man of penetrating psychological insight, who warned relentlessly against pride, to have been catastrophically self-deceived at the very centre of his self-understanding — and stranger still that the delusion left no other mark on a life his intimates judged blameless. The defender must concede that grandiosity and sanctity have, on rare occasions, coexisted. Can it be ruled out by logic alone? No. But the conjunction is improbable, and improbability is what evidential arguments trade in.

obj.q: You draw the lofty claims from the Gospels and the spotless character from the same Gospels. If they are reliable enough for one, why not trust them for deity directly — and if not, why trust the portrait?
obj.model: The argument need not treat the Gospels as uniformly reliable or wholly unreliable. On ordinary critical grounds — multiple attestation, the criterion of embarrassment, coherence with a first-century Jewish setting — the historian can grant that the broad moral character and the implicit authority-claims are well-rooted in the tradition, while staying more cautious about specific Johannine formulations. It takes what critical scholarship grants and asks what best explains it. Every link depends on source-judgments a reasonable person can weigh differently; but since the layered reading builds only on what critical scholarship already grants, it is the better reading, not merely a permitted one.

obj.q: Pick ‘liar.’ Founders exaggerate to mobilise people — a lie for a good cause is still a lie, and history is full of them.
obj.model: A calculated lie is shaped to be believed, and a first-century Jew inventing a messianic claim had a ready script: a widespread hope of the age was for a conquering son of David who would break the yoke of Rome. Jesus inverted it. He set at the centre not a throne but a cross — a death the Law itself called accursed, and which Paul concedes was “a stumbling block to Jews and folly to Gentiles.” A fraud angling to be received as Israel’s deliverer does not court the one outcome most certain to discredit him before the very people he is trying to win. And the argument does not even require that Jesus foresaw the manner of his death in detail. It requires only that a crucified messiah stood at the centre of the movement’s message from the first. This does not prove the claims true; it bears hard on the theory that they were a deliberate deception.

unseen.q: Of course his followers called him sinless — admirers write tributes. Ask his enemies and you would hear a very different story about the man.
unseen.model: His enemies’ charges are preserved: a sorcerer who “led Israel astray” (the Talmud, b. Sanhedrin 43a, a late text whose date and referent are disputed), one “leading the people astray,” a blasphemer, and in the pagan critic Celsus an illegitimate pretender who worked by trickery. What is striking is the shape of the accusation: the quarrel runs again and again to the source of his power, the truth of his claims, and the circumstances of his birth. What the sources never produce is a sustained indictment of his conduct toward others — a ledger of cruelty, greed, or exploitation. The nearest they come is the taunt “a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners,” a jibe at the company he kept. Even the charge of leading the people astray, which does touch his honesty, was aimed at the fraud they alleged in his signs and claims, not at any record of how he treated the people around him. Tellingly, when Celsus reached for a personal failing he had to borrow one the Gospels had already reported on themselves, mocking his fear in Gethsemane. His enemies disputed who Jesus was; they did not compile the record of sordid deeds a genuinely vicious life would have left behind. These witnesses are weighed lightly, since the surviving record is thin and late; the support is corroborative rather than decisive.
